An overview of these foundational concepts is given in the subsections that follow to summarize the “how” and “why” of the Phase III research findings. A more detailed analysis and discussion will be addressed in subsequent editions of the AMD implementation report series. 4.1 Impacts and Implications of On-Demand Transit on AMD Operations Figure 22 illustrates the envisioned future when multiple AV fleet operating modes and vehicle technologies are deployed within an AMD. This figure provides some sense of the operational complexity that will be faced as these various vehicle technology fleets interact. BRT = bus rapid transit Source: Houston-Galveston Area Council The operational complexity of AV fixed-route transit is relatively low—analogous to traditional fixed-route transit where boarding and alighting occur on a fixed schedule and at fixed locations, with vehicles stopping at every station. However, the trend for transit agencies across the country is to integrate ODT modes into the public mobility service offerings. 39 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. ODT has grown significantly in the past decade, as indicated in Figure 23 (from a prominent industry source for ODT data3). Starting with initial pilots in 2014 and 2015 and using business models and software algorithms pioneered in the TNC industry, public mobility began to experiment with app-based on-demand service. The transition of pilot ODT services to commercial offerings coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic when TNCs and ODT were found to adjust to sparse demand better than fixed-route transit and complement fixed-route transit service in higher-density areas. NLR research into ODT spanned rural (Weigl et al. 2022; Powell et al. 2023), suburban (Powell et al. 2024), and urban areas (Esteban et al. 2024). In low-density areas, ODT was found to outperform fixed-route transit for community circulation services. For higher-density urban areas, ODT provided both highly responsive community circulation services and effective FMLM service to regional fixed-route transit. The continued rapid growth of ODT in sparse development density and to complement fixed-route services in dense urban areas, coupled with the rapid adoption of commercial ride-hailing services, points to the anticipation that ODT services and TNCs—both using AV and EV technology—will be a primary component of future AMDs.
